2. The air in a kitchen has pressure $1.0 \times 10^5$ Pa and temperature 22°C. A refrigerator of internal volume 0.36 m$^3$ is installed in the kitchen.
(a) With the door open the air in the refrigerator is initially at the same temperature and pressure as the air in the kitchen. Calculate the number of molecules of air in the refrigerator. [2]
(b) The refrigerator door is closed. The air in the refrigerator is cooled to 5.0°C and the number of air molecules in the refrigerator stays the same.
(i) Determine the pressure of the air inside the refrigerator. [2]
(ii) The door of the refrigerator has an area of 0.72 m$^2$. Show that the minimum force needed to open the refrigerator door is about 4 kN. [2]
(iii) Comment on the magnitude of the force in (b)(ii). [2]

[Graph: y / cm (−6 to 6) against x / m (0.0 to 1.0); solid sinusoid of amplitude 4 cm, wavelength 0.30 m; dotted wave shifted 0.05 m to the right; particle P at y = 0 near x = 0.23 m, particle Q at y = 4 cm near x = 0.30 m]
(a) (i) Calculate, in m s$^{-1}$, the speed for this wave. [1]
(ii) Calculate, in Hz, the frequency for this wave. [2]

(c) One end of a string is attached to an oscillator and the other is fixed to a wall. When the frequency of the oscillator is 360 Hz the standing wave shown is formed on the string.
[Diagram: string of length 2.1 m between an oscillator and a wall, showing a standing wave with three loops (third harmonic)]
Point X (not shown) is a point on the string at a distance of 10 cm from the oscillator.
(i) State the number of all other points on the string that have the same amplitude and phase as X. [1]
(ii) The frequency of the oscillator is reduced to 120 Hz. On the diagram, draw the standing wave that will be formed on the string. [1]
[Diagram: blank 2.1 m string between oscillator and wall]

[Diagram: field into page (crosses); proton on the right of a dotted circular path with velocity arrow pointing upward]

(ii) Calculate the time for one complete revolution. [2]
(c) Explain why the kinetic energy of the proton is constant. [2]

8. (a) In a classical model of the singly-ionized helium atom, a single electron orbits the nucleus in a circular orbit of radius $r$.
[Diagram: electron moving on a dashed circular orbit of radius r around the helium nucleus]
(i) Show that the speed $v$ of the electron with mass $m$, is given by $v = \sqrt{\frac{2ke^2}{mr}}$. [1]
(ii) Hence, deduce that the total energy of the electron is given by $E_{TOT} = -\frac{ke^2}{r}$. [2]
(iii) In this model the electron loses energy by emitting electromagnetic waves. Describe the predicted effect of this emission on the orbital radius of the electron. [2]
(b) The Bohr model for hydrogen can be applied to the singly-ionized helium atom. In this model the radius $r$, in m, of the orbit of the electron is given by $r = 2.7 \times 10^{-11} \times n^2$ where $n$ is a positive integer.
(i) Show that the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ of the electron in the $n = 3$ state is $\lambda = 5.1 \times 10^{-10}$ m. The formula for the de Broglie wavelength of a particle is $\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$. [2]
(ii) Estimate for $n = 3$, the ratio $\frac{\text{circumference of orbit}}{\text{de Broglie wavelength of electron}}$. State your answer to one significant figure. [1]
(c) The description of the electron is different in the Schrodinger theory than in the Bohr model. Compare and contrast the description of the electron according to the Bohr model and to the Schrodinger theory. [3]

[Circuit: capacitor X, open switch S, capacitor Y and a resistor in a single loop]
(a) Calculate, in J, the energy stored in X with the switch S open. [2]
(b) The capacitance of Y is 12 µF. S is now closed.
(i) Calculate the final charge on X and the final charge on Y. [3]
(ii) Calculate the final total energy, in J, stored in X and Y. [2]

10. The lens of an optical system is coated with a thin film of magnesium fluoride of thickness $d$. Monochromatic light of wavelength 656 nm in air is incident on the lens. The angle of incidence is $\theta$. Two reflected rays, X and Y, are shown.
[Diagram: ray incident at angle θ on a magnesium fluoride layer of thickness d on top of a lens; ray X reflected from the top surface, ray Y reflected from the film–lens boundary]
The following refractive indices are available.
Air = 1.00
Magnesium fluoride = 1.38
Lens = 1.58
(a) Predict whether reflected ray X undergoes a phase change. [2]
(b) The thickness of the magnesium fluoride film is $d$. For the case of normal incidence ($\theta = 0$),
(i) state, in terms of $d$, the path difference between the reflected rays X and Y. [1]
(ii) calculate the smallest value of $d$ that will result in destructive interference between ray X and ray Y. [2]
(iii) discuss a practical advantage of this arrangement. [2]
(c) Light from a point source is incident on the pupil of the eye of an observer. The diameter of the pupil is 2.8 mm.
(i) Draw, on the axes, the variation with diffraction angle of the intensity of light incident on the retina of the observer. [2]
[Blank axes: Intensity against Diffraction angle]
(ii) Estimate, in rad, the smallest angular separation of two distinct point sources of light of wavelength 656 nm that can be resolved by the eye of this observer. [2]
